newsitem.title: USA: Miami oversight board ready to approve budget.
newsitem.headline: Miami oversight board ready to approve budget.

text.p: Florida Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay said Monday that the state oversight board he chairs probably will approve Miami's five-year budget bailout plan at its next meeting on May 12.
"I feel we are past the areas of major substantive concern," MacKay told Reuters after the city submitted a revised five-year plan Monday.

The latest plan eliminates all projected deficits through 2002, relying on a newly approved fire-rescue fee, leases of city property, new ad valorem tax revenues from public-private partnerships, and operating efficiencies such as the re-bidding of workers compsensation and health care contracts.
It also leaves open the possibility of privatizing the city's solid waste department.
The plan erases projected deficits of up to $46 million a year, creating projected surplusses of up to $1.9 million a year.
MacKay said the board still had some technical concerns, specifically a pending outside audit of the city's 1996 fiscal year.
Jose Gonzalez, who heads the KPMG Peat Marwick team conducting the audit, said it would confirm that Miami ended fiscal 1996 on September 30 with a $44 million deficit.

But he said the audit cannot be finished until Miami's bond counsel submits a letter addressing whether the city violated any of bond covenents by borrowing between its restricted and unrestricted funds.
"That's been a major piece that we've been waiting for," board member Cynthia Curry said.
MacKay said the board could accept the budget plan, contingent upon a favorable audit, when it votes on the plan on May 12.
Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the oversight board in December to help Miami erase a $68 million deficit for fiscal 1997, and eliminate recurring structural deficits.

The city was required to submit a balanced five-year budget by April 15, but the plan it submitted still had annual deficits for 1998 through 2001. City commissioners approved revisions Monday morning and sent the latst plan to the board.
While board members still expressed concerns about the training of city financial staff and its auditing proceedures, they praised the revised version.
"I think you can see that we're much more comfortable than we were last time," MacKay said.
"It really looks like a good plan," said Gail Sitting, one of the governor's financial officers who has been working closely with the city.
